public import FormalConjecturesUtil

/-!
# Erdős Problem 779

*Reference:* [erdosproblems.com/779](https://www.erdosproblems.com/779)
-/

@[expose] public section

open Finset Nat

namespace Erdos779

/--
A Conjecture of Marian Deaconescu, see p.120 in https://doi.org/10.2307/2975810

[Needed to index shift in order to avoid trivial case $n = 0$,
where the conjecture is trivially false.]
-/
-- TODO(firsching): add formalization of the known cases for this conjecture:
-- n ≤ 1000, as well as the conjecture that p ≤ n^O(1)
@[category research open, AMS 11]
theorem erdos_779 (n : ℕ) (hn : n ≥ 1): let P := ∏ i ∈ range (n + 1), nth Nat.Prime i
    ∃ p, p.Prime ∧ (P + p).Prime ∧ nth Nat.Prime n < p ∧ p < P := by
  sorry

end Erdos779

reformulations.difference: The source uses one-based primes p₁,…,p_N with N > 1. Lean instead quantifies n ≥ 1, forms the product of Nat.nth Nat.Prime i for 0 ≤ i ≤ n, and uses Nat.nth Nat.Prime n as the strict lower bound for p.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: Set N = n + 1. Because Nat.nth is zero-indexed, Nat.nth Nat.Prime i = p_{i+1}. Thus the product is exactly p₁⋯p_N, the lower bound is p_N, and n ≥ 1 corresponds bijectively to N > 1. Both primality conditions and the strict upper bound remain identical. In /workspace/review/scratch.lean, Review779.actual_statement_equivalence proves an equivalence between the imported theorem's actual type and the source-shaped statement with a product over Finset.Icc 1 N. Its proof has no sorryAx dependency.

review.notes: The sole declaration faithfully states the cited problem, which the source still records as open. Checked Nat.nth's definition and proved that its out-of-range default cannot arise for primes. Lean verifies the first four permitted cases, with (P,p) = (6,5), (30,7), (210,13), (2310,23), and refutes the excluded n = 0 case. The Guy article's full text was inaccessible; its bibliographic details were verified, and the complete precise mathematical statement was available on the cited Erdős Problems page.
